resources.string: Ear canal cutaway
Auricle and ear canal, from the outer rim to the eardrum
Helix
This rolled cartilage rim curves around the upper and back edges of the auricle.
Concha
This deep bowl of the auricle funnels sound toward the opening of the ear canal, beside the tragus.
Ear canal
The canal curves inward from the concha. Its outer portion is supported by cartilage; its inner portion runs through the temporal bone.
Eardrum
The thin, slanted tympanic membrane closes the inner end of the canal and separates it from the middle ear.
Bony labyrinth
Inner ear in oblique view: canals, vestibule, cochlea and nerve
Semicircular canals
Three bony loops lie in different planes and house ducts that sense head rotation. The two upright canals share one limb near the vestibule.
Vestibule
This chamber lies between the semicircular canals and cochlea. It houses the utricle and saccule, which sense linear motion and head tilt.
Vestibulocochlear nerve
Vestibular and cochlear fibers run together through the internal acoustic canal toward the brainstem, carrying balance and hearing signals.
Nasal wall cutaway
Side view of the nose, with the septum removed to reveal one lateral wall
Nasal vestibule
Just inside the nostril, this short skin-lined entrance leads back into the nasal cavity.
Middle nasal concha
This curved shelf on the side wall lies between the smaller superior concha and the larger inferior concha. The passage directly beneath it is the middle meatus.
Inferior nasal concha
The lowest and largest shelf runs above the hard palate. The nasal passage opens behind it into the nasopharynx.
Dorsal cutaway
Tongue from above, with the root at the top and a muscle cutaway along one side
Lingual tonsil
Small clusters of lymphoid tissue form low nodules in the mucosa of the tongue root, behind the terminal sulcus.
Terminal sulcus
This V-shaped groove points back toward the throat. It separates the front two-thirds of the tongue from the root.
Vallate papillae
These large, ringed papillae form a row just in front of the terminal sulcus. They contain microscopic taste buds, as do the smaller fungiform papillae scattered farther forward.
Intrinsic tongue muscle
Lengthwise, crosswise and vertical muscle fibers interweave beneath the surface. These fibers change the shape of the tongue.
